title: Κινήθη ἀγορή
titleEn: The Test and the Rush for the Ships — Iliad 2.84–181
part: The Test and the Rush for the Ships (2.84–181)
about: Nestor leads the kings out of the council, and the army pours from huts and ships to the assembly like swarms of bees, with Rumour, a messenger of Zeus, urging them on. Agamemnon stands with the sceptre that Hephaestus made and that came to him through Zeus, Hermes, Pelops, Atreus and Thyestes. In the test he planned, he tells the army that Zeus has deceived him and that they must sail home, for Troy will not now be taken. His words stir the assembly like a sea in a gale, and the men stampede to the ships and begin to haul them down to the water. Hera tells Athena that the flight would leave Helen to the Trojans, and Athena goes down to Odysseus, who stands grieving by his ship, and bids him stop the army.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας βουλῆς ἐξῆρχε νέεσθαι,
οἳ δ’ ἐπανέστησαν πείθοντό τε ποιμένι λαῶν
σκηπτοῦχοι βασιλῆες·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way out of the council, and the sceptred kings rose and obeyed the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then having spoken’ closes Nestor’s speech, and Nestor is the subject of ἐξῆρχε, the imperfect of ἐξάρχω ‘lead off’: βουλῆς ‘from the council’ is a genitive, νέεσθαι ‘to go’ an infinitive. οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’ (the article as a pronoun) and ἐπανέστησαν the aorist of ἐπανίστημι ‘rise up’, used intransitively; πείθοντο takes the dative ποιμένι λαῶν ‘the shepherd of the people’, a title that most often belongs to Agamemnon, whom the kings follow out of the council, though the line does not name him. σκηπτοῦχοι βασιλῆες ‘sceptre-bearing kings’ is a stock phrase for the chiefs, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t: ἐπεσσεύοντο δὲ λαοί.
sentences.l: and rushed on, the people.
sentences.i: and the people came rushing on.
sentences.n: ἐπεσσεύοντο is the imperfect of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush on, hurry up’, with the doubled σ of epic verse; its subject λαοί ‘people’ follows it, so the verb comes first. The kings have risen; now the common army moves, and the simile that follows pictures it.

sentences.t:
ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἁδινάων
πέτρης ἐκ γλαφυρῆς αἰεὶ νέον ἐρχομενάων,
βοτρυδὸν δὲ πέτονται ἐπ’ ἄνθεσιν εἰαρινοῖσιν·
sentences.i: As swarms of thronging bees go out of a hollow rock, new ones always coming, and fly in clusters over the flowers of spring;
sentences.n: ἠΰτε ‘as, like’ opens a simile that runs on through line 90 and is taken up at 91 by ὣς τῶν ‘so of them’. ἔθνεα ‘tribes’ is the word for any company that moves together; here it means swarms of bees. εἶσι (from εἶμι ‘go’) is singular beside the neuter plural ἔθνεα, which Greek allows. μελισσάων ἁδινάων and ἐρχομενάων are genitive plurals in the epic ending -άων (Attic -ῶν); ἁδινός means ‘thick, crowded’. νέον is an adverb, ‘anew’, so ‘ever newly coming’ means that fresh bees keep emerging. γλαφυρῆς is ‘hollow’, as of caves. βοτρυδόν ‘in clusters’ comes from βότρυς ‘bunch of grapes’; εἰαρινοῖσιν is the epic dative of εἰαρινός ‘of spring’.

sentences.t: αἳ μέν τ’ ἔνθα ἅλις πεποτήαται, αἳ δέ τε ἔνθα·
sentences.l: some of them here in crowds have flown about, and others there;
sentences.i: some are flying in crowds here, others there;
sentences.n: αἳ μέν … αἳ δέ ‘some … others’ (the article as a pronoun), with τε of general statement. ἅλις is ‘in crowds, in plenty’. πεποτήαται is the perfect of ποτάομαι ‘fly’ in an epic form, ‘have taken wing and are on the wing’. The line sets out the bees’ pattern, some here in crowds and others there, and the next line applies it to the men.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν ἔθνεα πολλὰ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων
ἠϊόνος προπάροιθε βαθείης ἐστιχόωντο
ἰλαδὸν εἰς ἀγορήν·
sentences.i: so, from the ships and the huts, in front of the deep shore, their many swarms came marching in troops to the assembly;
sentences.n: ὣς τῶν ‘so of them’ returns from the simile to the men, and ἔθνεα picks up the word of line 87, now for companies of soldiers. νεῶν ἄπο is ἀπὸ νεῶν, with the preposition placed after its noun and the accent thrown back (anastrophe). κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισίη ‘hut’, the shelter that each company has beside its ship. ἠϊόνος … βαθείης ‘the deep shore’ is a shelving beach, and προπάροιθε ‘in front of’ governs it. ἐστιχόωντο is the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘march in rows’, in an open epic form; ἰλαδόν ‘in troops’ comes from ἴλη ‘troop, band’. The edition puts an ano teleia after ἀγορήν.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφισιν ὄσσα δεδήει
ὀτρύνουσ’ ἰέναι Διὸς ἄγγελος·
sentences.l:
and among them a rumour was blazing,
urging them to go, a messenger of Zeus;
sentences.i: and among them a rumour burned bright, urging them to go, a messenger of Zeus;
sentences.n: μετὰ δέ σφισιν ὄσσα δεδήει: ὄσσα is ‘voice, report, rumour’, and δεδήει is the pluperfect of δαίω ‘blaze’, ‘had flared up, was ablaze’; σφισιν ‘among them’. Printed with a small letter here, the word is still treated as a power: Zeus sends it, as Διὸς ἄγγελος ‘a messenger of Zeus’ says, and it goes through the army urging (ὀτρύνουσ’, the participle with its last vowel dropped; ἰέναι ‘to go’) without any human speaker.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἀγέροντο.
sentences.l: and they gathered.
sentences.i: and they gathered.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’, with ἀγέροντο, the aorist of ἀγείρομαι ‘gather’ without its augment (the same verb as ἤγερθεν at 1.57). The short sentence completes the movement of the army, and the next line turns to the noise of its sitting down.

sentences.t:
τετρήχει δ’ ἀγορή, ὑπὸ δὲ στεναχίζετο γαῖα
λαῶν ἱζόντων, ὅμαδος δ’ ἦν·
sentences.l:
And the assembly was in turmoil, and beneath groaned the earth
as the people sat down, and there was an uproar;
sentences.i: The assembly was in turmoil, and the earth groaned beneath the people as they sat down, and there was an uproar;
sentences.n: τετρήχει is the pluperfect of ταράσσω (the old perfect is τέτρηχα, ‘be in turmoil’), so ‘was in turmoil’. ὑπὸ … στεναχίζετο: ὑπό is an adverb ‘beneath’, and στεναχίζετο the imperfect of στεναχίζω ‘groan’. λαῶν ἱζόντων is a genitive absolute, ‘with the people sitting down’, from ἵζω ‘sit’. ὅμαδος ‘din, uproar’ is the noise of a crowd.

sentences.t:
ἐννέα δέ σφεας
κήρυκες βοόωντες ἐρήτυον, εἴ ποτ’ ἀϋτῆς
σχοίατ’, ἀκούσειαν δὲ διοτρεφέων βασιλήων.
sentences.l:
and nine
heralds, shouting, were restraining them, in case they might ever from clamour
hold back, and hear the Zeus-nurtured kings.
sentences.i: Nine heralds, crying out, kept trying to hold them back, in the hope that they might stop their clamour and listen to the Zeus-nurtured kings.
sentences.n: ἐννέα δέ σφεας … ἐρήτυον: σφεας is the epic accusative ‘them’, and ἐρήτυον the imperfect of ἐρητύω ‘restrain’, here a repeated effort, ‘kept trying to hold back’. βοόωντες is the participle of βοάω ‘shout’ in an open epic form. εἴ ποτ’ ἀϋτῆς σχοίατ’, ἀκούσειαν δέ: the optatives σχοίατο (aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘hold oneself back from’, with the genitive ἀϋτῆς ‘clamour’) and ἀκούσειαν give the heralds’ hope, ‘in case they might stop their shouting and listen’. διοτρεφέων βασιλήων ‘Zeus-nurtured kings’ is a stock phrase, genitive after ἀκούω.

sentences.t:
σπουδῇ δ’ ἕζετο λαός, ἐρήτυθεν δὲ καθ’ ἕδρας
παυσάμενοι κλαγγῆς·
sentences.l:
With difficulty the people sat down, and were held back to their seats,
having ceased from the din;
sentences.i: With difficulty the people sat down, and were held back in their seats, and ceased their din;
sentences.n: σπουδῇ is ‘with effort, with difficulty’ here (the same word can mean ‘in haste’); ἕζετο is the imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’, here ‘sat down’, and λαός is a singular, ‘the people’. ἐρήτυθεν is the 3rd plural aorist passive of ἐρητύω, ‘were held back’, the verb of the heralds’ work in the line before; καθ’ ἕδρας ‘in (to) their seats’. παυσάμενοι κλαγγῆς ‘having ceased from the din’ takes the genitive; κλαγγή is a sharp, ringing cry. The edition puts an ano teleia after κλαγγῆς.

sentences.t:
ἀνὰ δὲ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἔστη σκῆπτρον ἔχων τὸ μὲν Ἥφαιστος κάμε τεύχων.
sentences.l:
and up lord Agamemnon
stood, holding the sceptre which Hephaestus toiled making.
sentences.i: Then lord Agamemnon stood up, holding the sceptre that Hephaestus had toiled to make.
sentences.n: ἀνὰ δὲ … ἔστη is tmesis (the verb split from its prefix): ἀνέστη ‘stood up’, with κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων between. κρείων ‘ruling’ is translated ‘lord’, so ‘lord Agamemnon’. σκῆπτρον ἔχων ‘holding the sceptre’; τό is the relative ‘which’, and κάμε is the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’, with the participle τεύχων ‘making’: ‘which Hephaestus toiled making’. The sceptre is the sign of command, and the next lines trace it back to its maker.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστος μὲν δῶκε Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι,
αὐτὰρ ἄρα Ζεὺς δῶκε διακτόρῳ ἀργεϊφόντῃ·
sentences.l:
Hephaestus gave it to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord,
and then Zeus gave it to the guide, Argeïphontes;
sentences.i: Hephaestus gave it to lord Zeus, the son of Cronus, and Zeus gave it to the guide, the slayer of Argus;
sentences.n: A chain of gifts begins: Hephaestus → Zeus → Hermes → Pelops → Atreus → Thyestes → Agamemnon, each gift told in a line or half-line. δῶκε is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι. Διὶ Κρονίωνι ἄνακτι ‘to Zeus, the son of Cronus, the lord’ (Κρονίων is a patronymic like Κρονίδης); the μέν here is answered by αὐτάρ, ‘and then’. Hermes is named by two stock epithets in the dative: διακτόρῳ ‘the guide’ (meaning of διάκτορος not known) and ἀργεϊφόντῃ ‘slayer of Argus’ (meaning of ἀργεϊφόντης disputed).

sentences.t:
Ἑρμείας δὲ ἄναξ δῶκεν Πέλοπι πληξίππῳ,
αὐτὰρ ὃ αὖτε Πέλοψ δῶκ’ Ἀτρέϊ ποιμένι λαῶν,
sentences.l:
and Hermes the lord gave it to Pelops, the horse-lashing,
and he in turn, Pelops, gave it to Atreus, shepherd of the people,
sentences.i: and the lord Hermes gave it to Pelops, the horse-lasher, and Pelops in turn gave it to Atreus, shepherd of the people,
sentences.n: Ἑρμείας δὲ ἄναξ: here Hermes is ἄναξ ‘lord’, as Zeus was at 102. πληξίππῳ is the dative of πληξίππος ‘horse-lashing’, from πλήσσω ‘strike’ and ἵππος ‘horse’. αὐτὰρ ὃ αὖτε Πέλοψ is ‘and he, Pelops, in turn’ (ὅ is a pronoun with the name added after it). Ἀτρέϊ is the epic dative of Ἀτρεύς, and ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is Atreus’s title, as it is Agamemnon’s. The sentence runs on through line 108 and is cut at this comma only because it is long.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεὺς δὲ θνῄσκων ἔλιπεν πολύαρνι Θυέστῃ,
αὐτὰρ ὃ αὖτε Θυέστ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι λεῖπε φορῆναι,
πολλῇσιν νήσοισι καὶ Ἄργεϊ παντὶ ἀνάσσειν.
sentences.l:
and Atreus, dying, left it to Thyestes, rich in lambs,
and he in turn, Thyestes, left it to Agamemnon to bear,
to be lord over many islands and all Argos.
sentences.i: and Atreus, as he died, left it to Thyestes, rich in lambs, and Thyestes in turn left it to Agamemnon to carry, so that he might rule over many islands and all Argos.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεὺς δὲ θνῄσκων ‘Atreus, dying’, with ἔλιπεν the aorist of λείπω ‘leave’. πολύαρνι is the dative of πολύαρνος ‘rich in lambs’, from ἀρήν ‘lamb’, an epithet for a man rich in flocks. Θυέστ’ has its final vowel dropped; λεῖπε is the imperfect, ‘left’. φορῆναι is the epic infinitive of φορέω ‘carry, bear’, and ἀνάσσειν ‘to be lord’ follows with the datives πολλῇσιν νήσοισι and Ἄργεϊ παντί ‘over many islands and all Argos’. Ἄργος can mean a wider land than the city; the Greek does not fix its limits.

sentences.t: τῷ ὅ γ’ ἐρεισάμενος ἔπε’ Ἀργείοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: Leaning on it, he spoke words among the Argives:
sentences.i: Leaning on it, he spoke these words among the Argives:
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘on it’, the sceptre; ὅ γ’ is ‘he’; ἐρεισάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐρείδομαι ‘lean’. ἔπε’ is ἔπεα ‘words’ with its last vowel dropped. Ἀργείοισι μετηύδα ‘spoke among the Argives’ is a speech-introduction (μετηύδα, aorist of μεταυδάω), and ‘Argives’ here means the whole army. The speech that follows is the test Agamemnon announced to the elders in the previous part (2.73–75): he says the opposite of what he means, to see what the army will do.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος
Ζεύς με μέγα Κρονίδης ἄτῃ ἐνέδησε βαρείῃ,
sentences.l:
“O friends, heroes, Danaans, attendants of Ares,
Zeus me greatly, the son-of-Cronus, in bewilderment has bound, heavy;
sentences.i: “Friends, Danaan heroes, attendants of Ares: Zeus, the son of Cronus, has bound me hard in heavy bewilderment,
sentences.n: The edition prints no stops in the address ὦ φίλοι ἥρωες Δαναοὶ θεράποντες Ἄρηος, so it is a string of vocatives: ‘friends, heroes, Danaans, attendants of Ares’. θεράπων is ‘attendant’, so the soldiers are Ares’ attendants in battle. Ἄρηος is the epic genitive of Ἄρης. Ζεύς με … ἐνέδησε: ἐνέδησε is the aorist of ἐνδέω ‘bind in’, with μέγα ‘greatly’ and the dative ἄτῃ … βαρείῃ ‘in heavy bewilderment’; ἄτη is a clouding of the mind that brings ruin, and here Agamemnon puts it down to Zeus. Κρονίδης is the patronymic ‘son of Cronus’.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιος, ὃς πρὶν μέν μοι ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσεν
Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντ’ εὐτείχεον ἀπονέεσθαι,
sentences.l:
cruel one, who before indeed promised me and nodded assent
that Ilios, well-walled, having sacked-utterly, I should return home;
sentences.i: cruel one, who before promised me, and pledged it with a nod, that I should sack well-walled Ilios and return home;
sentences.n: σχέτλιος ‘cruel’ is nominative, in apposition to Ζεύς; ὃς πρὶν μέν looks for the νῦν δέ of the next line, ‘who before … but now’. ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσεν ‘promised and nodded assent’, a pair of aorists, the nod being Zeus’s pledge. Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντ’ εὐτείχεον ἀπονέεσθαι: ἐκπέρσαντ’ is an accusative participle agreeing with an unstated ‘me’, the subject of the infinitive ἀπονέεσθαι ‘go back home’, so ‘that I should sack well-walled Ilios and go home’. Ἴλιον is a second name for Troy (see 141); εὐτείχεον is an older uncontracted form of εὐτείχεος ‘well-walled’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ κακὴν ἀπάτην βουλεύσατο, καί με κελεύει
δυσκλέα Ἄργος ἱκέσθαι, ἐπεὶ πολὺν ὤλεσα λαόν.
sentences.l:
but now an evil deceit he has devised, and bids me
inglorious to Argos to come, since a great host I have lost.
sentences.i: but now he has devised an evil deceit, and bids me return to Argos without glory, since I have lost so many of my people.
sentences.n: νῦν δὲ answers the πρὶν μέν before it. βουλεύσατο is the aorist middle of βουλεύω ‘plan, devise’, and κακὴν ἀπάτην ‘an evil deceit’ is Agamemnon’s word for what he now says Zeus has done; the reader knows the Dream of the previous part was exactly such a deceit, and that he is not telling the army the whole truth. δυσκλέα is the accusative agreeing with με, ‘without glory’. Ἄργος ἱκέσθαι ‘to come to Argos’ has the place as a plain accusative (ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι). ὤλεσα is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’, and πολὺν λαόν a singular, ‘a great host’.

sentences.t:
οὕτω που Διὶ μέλλει ὑπερμενέϊ φίλον εἶναι,
ὃς δὴ πολλάων πολίων κατέλυσε κάρηνα
ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ λύσει·
sentences.i: So, I suppose, it is bound to be dear to Zeus of surpassing strength, who has overthrown the heads of many cities and will overthrow more;
sentences.n: οὕτω που … μέλλει … εἶναι ‘so, I suppose, it is bound to be’: μέλλει with the infinitive says what must follow, and που is ‘I suppose’. Διὶ … ὑπερμενέϊ is the dative with φίλον ‘dear to’; ὑπερμενής ‘of surpassing strength’ is a stock epithet. ὃς δὴ … κατέλυσε κάρηνα: κάρηνα is literally ‘heads’, here the heads of cities, their citadels and tops; πολλάων πολίων is the epic genitive plural. κατέλυσε (aorist of καταλύω ‘undo, bring down’) and λύσει (future of λύω ‘loosen, undo’) are the same verb, and the English keeps that. ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ ‘and still also’ gives the future.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον.
sentences.l: for of him the strength is greatest.
sentences.i: for his strength is greatest.
sentences.n: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον: τοῦ is the article as a pronoun, ‘of him’, here Zeus, and κράτος ‘strength’ is the noun for power to prevail. μέγιστον is the superlative of μέγας, the predicate, ‘greatest’. The γάρ gives the reason for yielding to Zeus.

sentences.t:
αἰσχρὸν γὰρ τόδε γ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι
μὰψ οὕτω τοιόνδε τοσόνδε τε λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
ἄπρηκτον πόλεμον πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι
ἀνδράσι παυροτέροισι, τέλος δ’ οὔ πώ τι πέφανται·
sentences.l:
For shameful is this, at least, even for those yet to come to hear,
that in vain, so, such a people, so great, of the Achaeans
a fruitless war to war, and to fight
with men fewer, and an end not yet at all has appeared;
sentences.i: For it is shameful, even for those yet to come to hear, that such a host of Achaeans, so great, should wage a fruitless war to no purpose, and fight against fewer men, and no end has yet appeared;
sentences.n: αἰσχρὸν … πυθέσθαι: the infinitive πυθέσθαι (aorist of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn, hear’) is what is ‘shameful’, and ἐσσομένοισι ‘for those yet to come’ is the dative of later men. What they would hear stands in an accusative and infinitive: λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν … πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι, ‘that a host of Achaeans wage war and fight’. μὰψ οὕτω ‘idly, so’ means to no purpose; τοιόνδε τοσόνδε τε ‘such and so great’ points at the army before him. ἄπρηκτον πόλεμον πολεμίζειν ‘to wage a fruitless war’ has the noun and the verb from one root, and ἄπρηκτον means ‘without result’. ἀνδράσι παυροτέροισι ‘against fewer men’ is a dative after μάχεσθαι (comparative of παῦρος ‘few’). πέφανται is the perfect passive of φαίνω ‘show’, ‘has shown itself’. The edition puts an ano teleia after πέφανται.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ κ’ ἐθέλοιμεν Ἀχαιοί τε Τρῶές τε
ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες ἀριθμηθήμεναι ἄμφω,
sentences.l:
For if we were willing, Achaeans and Trojans,
faithful oaths having cut, to be counted, both sides,
sentences.i: For if we were willing, Achaeans and Trojans, to swear faithful oaths and both be counted,
sentences.n: A mock proposal begins that runs to line 128: suppose both sides swore a truce and counted heads. εἴ περ γάρ κ’ ἐθέλοιμεν ‘for if we were willing’, with the optative; its answer is πολλαί κεν δεκάδες δευοίατο at 128. ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες ‘having cut faithful oaths’: ὅρκια τάμνειν ‘cut oaths’ is the idiom for making a sworn treaty, from the victim that was cut for it. ἀριθμηθήμεναι is the epic aorist passive infinitive of ἀριθμέω ‘count’, ‘to be counted’, and ἄμφω ‘both’ (sides).

sentences.t:
Τρῶας μὲν λέξασθαι ἐφέστιοι ὅσσοι ἔασιν,
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐς δεκάδας διακοσμηθεῖμεν Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.l:
the Trojans to pick out, as many as are hearth-holders,
and we should be marshalled into tens, we Achaeans,
sentences.i: the Trojans to pick out all who have homes in the city, while we Achaeans should be marshalled into tens,
sentences.n: Τρῶας μὲν λέξασθαι: the infinitive λέξασθαι (aorist middle of λέγω ‘pick out, count’) still depends on ἐθέλοιμεν; the Trojans would list themselves. ἐφέστιοι ὅσσοι ἔασιν ‘as many as are at the hearth’, those with a hearth and home in the city, so not the allies that Agamemnon turns to at 130. At ἡμεῖς δ’ the construction passes from infinitive to optative: διακοσμηθεῖμεν is the aorist passive optative of διακοσμέω ‘marshal’, with ἐς δεκάδας ‘into tens’, and the optative goes on at 127 (ἑλοίμεθα).

sentences.t:
Τρώων δ’ ἄνδρα ἕκαστοι ἑλοίμεθα οἰνοχοεύειν,
πολλαί κεν δεκάδες δευοίατο οἰνοχόοιο.
sentences.l:
and of the Trojans a man each of us should take, to pour the wine,
many tens would lack a wine-pourer.
sentences.i: and each ten of us picked a Trojan to pour the wine, many tens of us would have no cupbearer.
sentences.n: Τρώων δ’ ἄνδρα ἕκαστοι ἑλοίμεθα οἰνοχοεύειν: ἑλοίμεθα is the aorist middle optative of αἱρέω ‘take, choose’, ἕκαστοι is plural, so ‘each company of us’, and οἰνοχοεύειν ‘to pour wine’ is an infinitive of purpose. The answer to the whole ‘if’ follows: πολλαί κεν δεκάδες δευοίατο οἰνοχόοιο, where δευοίατο is the optative of δεύομαι ‘lack’, with the genitive οἰνοχόοιο, ‘would lack a wine-pourer’: there would be more Achaean tens than Trojans to serve them. The word οἰνοχόος is a servant who pours wine for a table.

sentences.t:
τόσσον ἐγώ φημι πλέας ἔμμεναι υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
Τρώων, οἳ ναίουσι κατὰ πτόλιν·
sentences.l:
So many more, I say, are the sons of the Achaeans
than the Trojans, who dwell in the city;
sentences.i: So much more numerous, I say, are the sons of the Achaeans than the Trojans who live in the city;
sentences.n: τόσσον ἐγώ φημι πλέας ἔμμεναι: πλέας is the epic accusative plural of πλείων ‘more’, ἔμμεναι the epic infinitive ‘to be’, and τόσσον ‘so much’ gives the degree. υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός, so ‘sons of the Achaeans’ means the men. Τρώων is a genitive of comparison, ‘than the Trojans’. κατὰ πτόλιν ‘in the city’ has πτόλις, the epic form of πόλις. The edition puts an ano teleia after πτόλιν.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπίκουροι
πολλέων ἐκ πολίων ἐγχέσπαλοι ἄνδρες ἔασιν,
οἵ με μέγα πλάζουσι καὶ οὐκ εἰῶσ’ ἐθέλοντα
Ἰλίου ἐκπέρσαι εὖ ναιόμενον πτολίεθρον.
sentences.l:
but allies
from many cities, spear-brandishing men, there are,
who greatly drive me astray, and do not allow, though I wish,
of Ilios to sack-utterly the well-inhabited citadel.
sentences.i: but there are allies from many cities, spear-brandishing men, who drive me far off course and will not let me, for all my wish, sack the well-inhabited citadel of Ilios.
sentences.n: ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ are men who come to help; the Trojan allies are the point of the sentence. πολλέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of πολύς. ἐγχέσπαλοι ‘spear-brandishing’ is formed from ἔγχος ‘spear’ and a verb taken to be πάλλω ‘brandish’; the formation is not certain. οἵ με μέγα πλάζουσι: πλάζω ‘drive off course’, here meant of men who throw him off his course, ‘baffle, thwart’; οὐκ εἰῶσ’ ἐθέλοντα ‘do not allow me, though I wish’ (εἰῶσι is the 3rd plural of ἐάω). Ἰλίου ἐκπέρσαι εὖ ναιόμενον πτολίεθρον: ἐκπέρσαι is the infinitive of ἐκπέρθω ‘sack’, and ‘well-inhabited citadel’ is the phrase of 1.164.

sentences.t:
ἐννέα δὴ βεβάασι Διὸς μεγάλου ἐνιαυτοί,
καὶ δὴ δοῦρα σέσηπε νεῶν καὶ σπάρτα λέλυνται·
sentences.l:
Nine years of great Zeus have already gone by,
and now the timbers of the ships have rotted and the ropes are loosened;
sentences.i: Nine of great Zeus’s years have now gone by, and the timbers of the ships have rotted, and the ropes have come undone;
sentences.n: ἐννέα δὴ βεβάασι … ἐνιαυτοί: βεβάασι is the perfect of βαίνω ‘go’, and ἐνιαυτοί ‘years’, the word for a full cycle; Διὸς μεγάλου ‘of great Zeus’ makes the years his. καὶ δὴ … σέσηπε: σέσηπε is the perfect of σήπω ‘rot’, singular after the neuter plural δοῦρα ‘timbers’ (the same word is also ‘spears’). σπάρτα ‘ropes’ are cables of twisted plant fibre, and λέλυνται is the perfect passive of λύω ‘loosen’, ‘are slack’. The edition puts an ano teleia after λέλυνται.

sentences.t:
αἳ δέ που ἡμέτεραί τ’ ἄλοχοι καὶ νήπια τέκνα
εἵατ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροις ποτιδέγμεναι·
sentences.l:
and they, I suppose, our wives and infant children,
sit in the halls, waiting;
sentences.i: And our wives, I suppose, and our little children are sitting in the halls, waiting;
sentences.n: αἳ δέ που: αἳ is the article as a pronoun, ‘and they’, with που ‘I suppose’. ἡμέτεραί τ’ ἄλοχοι καὶ νήπια τέκνα ‘our wives and infant children’, the νήπιος being literally one who cannot yet speak. εἵατ’ is the 3rd plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’, with its last vowel dropped; ἐνὶ is ἐν, and ποτιδέγμεναι is the feminine plural participle of προσδέχομαι ‘wait for’, agreeing with the wives and children. Agamemnon turns from the army to the people at home.

sentences.t:
ἄμμι δὲ ἔργον
αὔτως ἀκράαντον οὗ εἵνεκα δεῦρ’ ἱκόμεσθα.
sentences.l:
and for us the task
just so unaccomplished is, for the sake of which we came here.
sentences.i: while for us the work stands just as it was, unaccomplished, the very work for which we came here.
sentences.n: ἄμμι is the epic dative of ἡμεῖς, ‘to us’. ἔργον … ἀκράαντον ‘an unaccomplished task’: ἀκράαντος is built on ἀ- and κραίνω ‘accomplish’. αὔτως ‘just so, as it was’ says there has been no progress. οὗ εἵνεκα is οὗ ἕνεκα ‘for which’, with the epic form εἵνεκα; δεῦρ’ is δεῦρο ‘here’, and ἱκόμεσθα the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘we came’, in an epic ending. The nine years are summed up in one clause: the job is not done.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: This line also stands in the Odyssey, there with commas that this edition leaves out. ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ‘but come’: ἄγεθ’ is ἄγετε with its vowel dropped and τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὡς. ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω ‘as I may say’ is a clause with ἄν and the aorist subjunctive; πειθώμεθα ‘let us obey’ is a hortative subjunctive, with ‘me’ understood, and πάντες ‘all of us’. Agamemnon asks first for obedience; what he will order is the lie at the centre of the test.

sentences.t: φεύγωμεν σὺν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.l: Let us flee with the ships to our dear fatherland;
sentences.i: let us flee with our ships to our dear fatherland;
sentences.n: φεύγωμεν is a hortative subjunctive, ‘let us flee’; νηυσί is the epic dative plural of ναῦς, ‘with our ships’. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘to our dear fatherland’: πατρίδα is an adjective, ‘of one’s fathers’, with γαῖαν ‘land’, and the phrase is stock; the line supplies no ‘our’, but the sense does. This is the order the test is meant to provoke.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔτι Τροίην αἱρήσομεν εὐρυάγυιαν.
sentences.l: for no longer shall we take Troy, wide-streeted.”
sentences.i: for we shall no longer take Troy of the wide streets.”
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔτι … αἱρήσομεν ‘for we shall no longer take’: αἱρήσομεν is the future of αἱρέω, here ‘capture (a city)’. Τροίην is the Ionic form of Τροίαν, and εὐρυάγυιαν ‘wide-streeted’ (εὐρύς ‘wide’ + ἀγυιά ‘street’) is a stock epithet of cities. The claim is the opposite of the Dream’s message, which told Agamemnon that Troy could now be taken. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοῖσι δὲ θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε
πᾶσι μετὰ πληθὺν ὅσοι οὐ βουλῆς ἐπάκουσαν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and in them the heart in their breasts he stirred,
in all through the crowd, as many as had not listened to the council;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he stirred the hearts in the breasts of all in the crowd, all who had not listened to the council;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ ends the speech. τοῖσι … πᾶσι ‘in all of them’ is a dative, split across the two lines, and θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ὄρινε ‘he stirred the heart in their breasts’ is a line-end formula (ὄρινε, aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’). μετὰ πληθύν ‘through the crowd’, ὅσοι οὐ βουλῆς ἐπάκουσαν ‘as many as had not listened to the council’: ἐπάκουσαν is the aorist of ἐπακούω, which takes the genitive βουλῆς. Only the elders had heard Agamemnon’s plan, so the rest take his order to flee at face value.

sentences.t:
κινήθη δ’ ἀγορὴ φὴ κύματα μακρὰ θαλάσσης
πόντου Ἰκαρίοιο, τὰ μέν τ’ Εὖρός τε Νότος τε
ὤρορ’ ἐπαΐξας πατρὸς Διὸς ἐκ νεφελάων.
sentences.l:
And the assembly was stirred, like the long waves of the sea,
of the Icarian open-sea, which the East Wind and the South Wind
rouse, rushing on, from the clouds of father Zeus.
sentences.i: The assembly was stirred like the long waves of the Icarian open sea, which the East Wind and the South Wind rouse, swooping on them out of the clouds of father Zeus.
sentences.n: κινήθη is the aorist passive of κινέω ‘move, stir’, and φή is a particle ‘like, as’. κύματα μακρά ‘long waves’ of πόντου Ἰκαρίοιο ‘the Icarian open sea’, the sea round the island of Icaria in the Aegean; πόντος is the open sea. τά is a relative ‘which’; Εὖρός τε Νότος τε are the East Wind and the South Wind, two subjects of the single verb ὤρορε (aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’). ἐπαΐξας is the aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush on, swoop on’, and πατρὸς Διὸς ἐκ νεφελάων ‘out of the clouds of father Zeus’ has the epic genitive plural νεφελάων.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε κινήσῃ Ζέφυρος βαθὺ λήϊον ἐλθὼν
λάβρος ἐπαιγίζων, ἐπί τ’ ἠμύει ἀσταχύεσσιν,
ὣς τῶν πᾶσ’ ἀγορὴ κινήθη·
sentences.i: And as when the West Wind comes and stirs a deep cornfield, swooping fiercely on it, and the grain bows down with its ears, so the whole assembly of them was stirred;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε … ‘and as when’ opens a second simile, of a field of grain. κινήσῃ is an aorist subjunctive without κε (usual in epic similes), ‘stirs’; Ζέφυρος is the West Wind, and βαθὺ λήϊον ‘deep (thick) standing grain’. ἐλθών ‘coming’; λάβρος ἐπαιγίζων ‘fierce, swooping on it’ (ἐπαιγίζω, ‘rush upon’). ἠμύει is from ἠμύω ‘bow down’, with the dative ἀσταχύεσσιν ‘with its ears of grain’; ἐπί is the adverb ‘down upon’. ὣς τῶν πᾶσ’ ἀγορὴ κινήθη ‘so of them the whole assembly was stirred’ brings the two similes back to the men. The edition puts an ano teleia after κινήθη.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἀλαλητῷ
νῆας ἔπ’ ἐσσεύοντο, ποδῶν δ’ ὑπένερθε κονίη
ἵστατ’ ἀειρομένη·
sentences.i: and with a shout they rushed to the ships, and the dust rose and stood in the air from beneath their feet;
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ ‘and they’ (the soldiers); ἀλαλητῷ is a dative of manner, ‘with a war-shout’. νῆας ἔπ’ is ἐπὶ νῆας, with the preposition after its noun and its last vowel dropped. ἐσσεύοντο, the same verb as ἐπεσσεύοντο at 86, now with the army running the other way. ποδῶν δ’ ὑπένερθε ‘from beneath their feet’; κονίη ‘dust’; ἵστατ’ ἀειρομένη is ἵστατο (imperfect middle of ἵστημι) with the participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’, ‘the dust stood, lifted’, a cloud hanging in the air.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἀλλήλοισι κέλευον
ἅπτεσθαι νηῶν ἠδ’ ἑλκέμεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν,
οὐρούς τ’ ἐξεκάθαιρον·
sentences.i: and they urged one another to lay hold of the ships and drag them down to the heavenly brine, and they cleared out the channels;
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ ἀλλήλοισι κέλευον ‘and they were urging one another’, the imperfect, followed by two infinitives: ἅπτεσθαι (with the genitive νηῶν, the epic form of νεῶν) ‘lay hold of’, and ἑλκέμεν, the epic infinitive of ἕλκω, ‘drag’. εἰς ἅλα δῖαν ‘into the heavenly brine’: ἅλς is the salt sea, and δῖος, ‘heavenly’, is the epithet that goes with it. οὐρούς τ’ ἐξεκάθαιρον: οὐρούς is a rare word, taken to mean the trenches or channels in which the hulls lay and were run down to the water; the sense comes from the context. ἐξεκάθαιρον is the imperfect of ἐκκαθαίρω ‘clean out’.

sentences.t:
ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκεν
οἴκαδε ἱεμένων·
sentences.l:
and the cry reached heaven
of those longing for home;
sentences.i: and the cry of the men longing for home reached heaven;
sentences.n: ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκεν ‘and the cry reached heaven’ is a stock expression for a very great noise; ἷκεν is the epic form of ἵκω ‘come to, reach’. οἴκαδε ἱεμένων: ἱεμένων is the genitive plural of the participle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager, long’, with οἴκαδε ‘for home’; it names the men whose cry it was. The edition puts an ano teleia after ἱεμένων.

sentences.t: ὑπὸ δ’ ᾕρεον ἕρματα νηῶν.
sentences.l: and from beneath they took away the props of the ships.
sentences.i: and they pulled the props from under the ships.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ δ’ ᾕρεον ἕρματα νηῶν: ὑπό is the adverb ‘from under’, and ᾕρεον the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘take’, ‘they were taking away’. ἕρματα are the props (stones or timbers) that held the hulls upright on the beach, and νηῶν is the epic genitive plural of ναῦς. With the props gone the ships can be run down.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν Ἀργείοισιν ὑπέρμορα νόστος ἐτύχθη
εἰ μὴ Ἀθηναίην Ἥρη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
Then for the Argives, beyond fate, a homecoming would have been made,
had not Hera spoken a word to Athena:
sentences.i: Then the Argives would have had a homecoming contrary to fate, had Hera not spoken to Athena:
sentences.n: ἔνθά κεν … ἐτύχθη: κεν with the aorist ἐτύχθη (aorist passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘come about’) says what would have happened, and the εἰ μή clause that follows names what prevented it. ὑπέρμορα ‘beyond fate’ is adverbial (ὑπέρ + μόρος ‘fate’), so the return would have gone against what was fated. νόστος ‘homecoming’. εἰ μὴ … ἔειπεν ‘if she had not spoken’: the indicative is regular after a κεν with the aorist; πρὸς … ἔειπεν is προσεῖπεν split (tmesis), ‘addressed’, with μῦθον as a cognate accusative and Ἀθηναίην as the person addressed; Ἥρη is the subject.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη,
οὕτω δὴ οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
Ἀργεῖοι φεύξονται ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης,
sentences.l:
“Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone,
so then, home to their dear fatherland
the Argives will flee, over the broad back of the sea,
sentences.i: “Ah, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone: so the Argives will flee home to their dear fatherland, over the sea’s broad back,
sentences.n: Hera’s speech begins (157–165). ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of dismay. αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη ‘child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone’ is a stock address to Athena: αἰγίοχος ‘aegis-bearing’ is of disputed meaning, and the meaning of Ἀτρυτώνη is not known. οἶκον δὲ is printed as two words and is οἴκαδε ‘homeward’. οὕτω δή ‘so then’ shows her dismay, and the sentence is put as a statement in the edition (Athena’s repeat of it at 174 is pointed as a question). φεύξονται is a future, ‘will flee’; ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης ‘over the broad back of the sea’ is stock, with νῶτα plural but picturing one surface. φίλην … πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘dear fatherland’ is stock, as at 140; the possessive ‘their’ is supplied from the sense.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δέ κεν εὐχωλὴν Πριάμῳ καὶ Τρωσὶ λίποιεν
Ἀργείην Ἑλένην, ἧς εἵνεκα πολλοὶ Ἀχαιῶν
ἐν Τροίῃ ἀπόλοντο φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης·
sentences.i: and would leave Argive Helen to Priam and the Trojans as a boast, Helen for whose sake many of the Achaeans have perished in Troy, far from their dear fatherland;
sentences.n: κὰδ δέ κεν … λίποιεν: κάδ is κατά before δ, and with λίποιεν it makes καταλίποιεν ‘leave behind’ (tmesis); κεν with the optative gives ‘would leave’, the result Hera expects from the flight. εὐχωλήν elsewhere means ‘vow, prayer’; here it is something to boast over (‘a boast’), left to Πριάμῳ καὶ Τρωσί. Ἀργείην Ἑλένην ‘Argive Helen’ (Ἀργείη, ‘Argive’, is a stock epithet of Helen); ἧς εἵνεκα ‘for whose sake’. ἀπόλοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι ‘perish’. φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης ‘from their dear fatherland’: πατρίδος is the adjective ‘of one’s fathers’, αἴης is the Ionic form of αἶα ‘land’, and the phrase is a variant of the stock φίλη πατρὶς αἶα. The edition puts an ano teleia after αἴης.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων·
sentences.l: But go now through the people of the bronze-shirted Achaeans;
sentences.i: But go now through the army of the bronze-shirted Achaeans;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν ‘but go now’ is the turn from complaint to command (ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι). κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν ‘through the host of the Achaeans’, with the stock epithet χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ (χαλκός ‘bronze’ + χιτών ‘tunic’, here the bronze armour), translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
σοῖς ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ἐρήτυε φῶτα ἕκαστον,
μηδὲ ἔα νῆας ἅλα δ’ ἑλκέμεν ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.l:
with your gentle words restrain each man,
and do not allow them to drag the both-sides-curving ships seaward.”
sentences.i: restrain each man with your gentle words, and do not let them drag the ships, curved on both sides, down to the sea.”
sentences.n: σοῖς ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ἐρήτυε φῶτα ἕκαστον ‘with your gentle words restrain each man’: ἐρήτυε is the imperative of ἐρητύω, the verb used of the heralds at 96, ἀγανός ‘gentle’, and φῶτα the accusative of φώς ‘man’. μηδὲ ἔα νῆας ἅλα δ’ ἑλκέμεν: ἔα is the imperative of ἐάω ‘allow’, the infinitive ἑλκέμεν has no stated subject (the men), and ἅλα δ’ is ἅλαδε ‘seaward’, printed as two words with the vowel dropped. ἀμφιελίσσας ‘curved on both sides’ (ἀμφί + ἑλίσσω ‘turn’) is a stock epithet of ships. Hera’s speech ends. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the third foot the short final syllable of νῆας has to be taken as long before the vowel of ἅλα.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων ἀΐξασα·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
and she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting;
sentences.i: So Hera spoke, and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, did not disobey; she went darting down from the peaks of Olympus;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so she spoke’, with οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ (the aorist of ἀπιθέω), a formula for a prompt response to a command. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’: γλαυκῶπις is a stock epithet (γλαυκός ‘gleaming’ + ὄψ ‘eye’), translated the same way every time. The second line also stands in the Odyssey; καρήνων is ‘peaks’ (heads of the mountain) and ἀΐξασα the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’.

sentences.t: καρπαλίμως δ’ ἵκανε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: Swiftly she reached the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Swiftly she came to the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: These words also occur in the previous part, where they describe the Dream’s journey to Agamemnon; here the subject is Athena, so the English has ‘she’. καρπαλίμως ‘swiftly’, ἵκανε ‘reached’ (ἱκάνω), θοὰς … νῆας ‘swift ships’, and ἐπί ‘to’, which stands between the adjective θοάς and its noun.

sentences.t:
εὗρεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον
ἑσταότ’·
sentences.l:
She found then Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning,
standing;
sentences.i: Then she found Odysseus, the equal of Zeus in cunning, standing there;
sentences.n: εὗρεν ἔπειτ’ ‘she found then’, with the aorist of εὑρίσκω. Ὀδυσῆα is Ὀδυσσῆα with a single σ for the metre. Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντον: ἀτάλαντος ‘equal in weight’ (from τάλαντον, a balance), with the dative Διί of comparison and μῆτιν an accusative of respect, ‘equal to Zeus in cunning’. ἑσταότ’ is ἑσταότα, the masculine accusative of the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’. Odysseus stands where he is while the others run.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅ γε νηὸς ἐϋσσέλμοιο μελαίνης
ἅπτετ’, ἐπεί μιν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἵκανεν·
sentences.l:
and he did not touch the well-benched black ship,
for grief had reached his heart and spirit;
sentences.i: and he did not lay a hand on his well-benched black ship, for grief had come upon his heart and spirit;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὅ γε … ἅπτετ’ ‘and he did not touch’: ἅπτετο is the imperfect middle of ἅπτομαι ‘lay hold of’, which takes the genitive νηὸς ἐϋσσέλμοιο μελαίνης ‘the well-benched black ship’ (ἐύσσελμος ‘with good benches’, μέλας ‘black’), a stock phrase for a ship. ἐπεί μιν ἄχος κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἵκανεν: μιν ‘him’; ἄχος ‘grief’ is the subject, and κραδίην καὶ θυμόν ‘heart and spirit’ the place it reaches; ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω. The line gives the reason he is not running with the rest.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And standing close by addressed him gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Gleaming-eyed Athena came and stood close beside him, and said to him:
sentences.n: This line also stands in the Odyssey. ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ‘and standing close’ (the present participle middle of ἵστημι), and προσέφη, the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’, the verb that opens a speech. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη again carries the stock epithet. The stop at the end of the line opens Athena’s speech.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
οὕτω δὴ οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
φεύξεσθ’ ἐν νήεσσι πολυκλήϊσι πεσόντες,
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
is it so, then, that home to your dear fatherland
you will flee, in your many-thwarted ships having fallen,
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, is it really so, then, that you will throw yourselves into your ships of many thwarts and flee home to your dear fatherland,
sentences.n: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is a stock address to Odysseus, also found in the Odyssey with a comma after Λαερτιάδη: διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’ (vocative), πολυμήχαν’ ‘of many devices’ with its vowel dropped. The question runs from here to the ; at 178. οὕτω δὴ οἶκον δὲ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν repeats 158 and has οἶκον δὲ as two words for οἴκαδε ‘homeward’. φεύξεσθ’ is φεύξεσθε, a second plural future: Athena speaks to Odysseus alone but of the whole army. ἐν νήεσσι πολυκλήϊσι πεσόντες ‘having fallen into your many-thwarted ships’, that is, tumbling in headlong, with νήεσσι the epic dative plural and πολυκλήϊσι ‘of many thwarts’ (κληΐς, the rowing-bench).

sentences.l:
and would you leave behind a boast for Priam and the Trojans,
Argive Helen, for whose sake many of the Achaeans
in Troy perished, away from their dear fatherland?
sentences.i: and would you leave Argive Helen to Priam and the Trojans as a boast, Helen for whose sake many of the Achaeans have perished in Troy, far from their dear fatherland?
sentences.n: The same words as 160–162, but with the second person λίποιτε ‘you would leave’ in place of Hera’s third person λίποιεν, and ended by the Greek question mark, so Athena puts it as a question where Hera made it a statement. For κὰδ … λίποιτε (tmesis), εὐχωλήν ‘a boast’, ἧς εἵνεκα and φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης see the first telling.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι νῦν κατὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν, μηδ’ ἔτ’ ἐρώει,
σοῖς δ’ ἀγανοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ἐρήτυε φῶτα ἕκαστον,
μηδὲ ἔα νῆας ἅλα δ’ ἑλκέμεν ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.l:
But go now through the people of the Achaeans, and no longer hold back,
and with your gentle words restrain each man,
and do not allow them to drag the both-sides-curving ships seaward.”
sentences.i: But go now through the army of the Achaeans, and no longer hang back; restrain each man with your gentle words, and do not let them drag the ships, curved on both sides, down to the sea.”
sentences.n: Lines 179–181 repeat Hera’s 163–165, with the epithet χαλκοχιτώνων dropped and an added μηδ’ ἔτ’ ἐρώει ‘and no longer hang back’ (ἐρώει is the imperative of ἐρωέω ‘draw back, hang back’), and with δ’ after σοῖς. For ἐρήτυε, ἀγανοῖς, ἔα, ἅλα δ’ and ἀμφιελίσσας see 164–165. Athena’s speech ends here. Line 181 is metrically irregular as transmitted, exactly as 165 is: in the third foot the short final syllable of νῆας has to be taken as long before the vowel of ἅλα.
